passage: Few school practices seem as commonsensical as grouping pupils by ability. A teacher facing a class whose members range from those who can barely read to those who devour novels must, it seems, either bore the strong or lose the weak, and sorting children into streams promises to spare her that dilemma. Each group can be taught at its own pace, with material pitched to its level; nobody is held back and nobody is left behind. The argument has the appeal of efficiency, and in a narrow sense it is often right.

The trouble lies in what a stream does after it has been formed. Placement usually happens early and rests on tests that measure, along with ability, a child's maturity, her familiarity with the kind of task being set and the amount of help she has had at home. Children who are young for their year are a familiar case: a few months' difference that would be invisible at fifteen can look like a difference of talent at seven. Once placed, however, pupils do not simply learn at different speeds. The lower streams are often given a thinner curriculum, less experienced teachers and quieter expectations, while the upper streams are prepared for examinations the others will never be entered for. The gap that the original test detected is thus widened by the arrangement that was supposed to respond to it, and the later results, which seem to confirm the placement, are partly its product.

Defenders of streaming reply that pupils can move between groups, and in principle they can. In practice movement is uncommon, and it is not difficult to see why. A child in a lower stream who has covered less material cannot readily join a group that has covered more, so even a genuine improvement in her understanding may never show up as a change of placement. Teachers, moreover, come to know their pupils as members of a particular set, and the label shapes how her work is read. The door is open, but the corridor behind it grows longer every term.

It would be a mistake to conclude that all grouping is harmful. Teaching a class of widely mixed attainment is genuinely demanding, and some arrangements avoid the worst effects of streaming: grouping pupils separately for particular subjects, regrouping them frequently and keeping the curriculum common, so that a move between groups remains a realistic possibility rather than a formal one. What distinguishes these arrangements from the rigid stream is not that they ignore differences in attainment but that they refuse to treat a single early measurement as a verdict.

passage: Most moral theories divide actions into three kinds: those we are required to do, those we are forbidden to do, and those that are merely permitted, yet ordinary moral thought seems to need a fourth. When a passer-by plunges into a freezing river to rescue a stranger, we do not say that she merely did something permitted, as though her act ranked alongside choosing tea over coffee. Nor do we say that she did her duty, for we would not have condemned her had she stayed on the riverbank and called for help. We say instead that she went beyond what duty asked. Acts of this kind are called supererogatory, and their existence has proved surprisingly awkward for theories that try to derive the whole of morality from a single principle.

The difficulty is sharpest for a simple form of consequentialism, the view that we are always required to do whatever produces the best outcome. On that view there is no room above duty, because the best available act is always the required one. If plunging into the river was the best thing she could do, she was obliged to do it; if it was not, she acted wrongly. Heroism disappears into ordinary obligation, and the person who fails to be a hero becomes a wrongdoer. Many critics take this to be a decisive objection: a theory that makes sainthood compulsory has misunderstood what morality is for.

Defenders reply that the objection confuses two questions: what one ought to do and what one may be blamed for not doing. Perhaps we should not blame the bystander who stays on the riverbank, since blaming people for failing to be heroes would be useless or cruel, while still holding that the rescue was what she ought to have done. This move is ingenious, and it does capture something; our reluctance to blame is partly practical. But it leaves the rescuer's own understanding of her act unexplained, for people who perform such acts often say, sincerely, that they had no choice, yet they rarely say that those who held back did wrong. Their sense of being called is personal, not a verdict on everyone.

What this suggests is that the space beyond duty is real but has a peculiar shape. It is not a zone of optional extras to which morality is indifferent, since such acts are admired precisely as moral achievements. Nor is it simply duty under a gentler name. It is the region where morality stops issuing demands to everyone and starts issuing invitations to particular people, and a theory that can speak only in demands will always misdescribe it.

passage: Long before there were central banks, people understood that a ruler who clipped the edges of coins, or mixed base metal into silver, was taking a share of his subjects' wealth without asking them. The modern version of the idea holds that a government which finances its spending by creating money imposes an inflation tax on everyone who holds that money. No law is passed and no collector calls; the price of bread simply rises, and the real value of the cash in people's pockets falls in proportion. In one respect the analogy with taxation is exact: resources move from the public to the issuer of money, who has spent the new money before its effect on prices is felt.

Critics of this practice argue that it is worse than ordinary taxation precisely because it is hidden: a tax on incomes must be proposed, debated and voted upon; an inflation tax requires only that the issuing authority do nothing to stop it. It also tends to fall heavily on those least able to protect themselves, such as households that keep their savings in cash or depend on incomes fixed in money terms, while it benefits anyone whose debts shrink in real value as prices rise. Among the largest such debtors, of course, is often the state itself.

The analogy misleads, however, when it is pressed too far. A tax is a deliberate choice, whereas much inflation arises from events that no government chose, such as a failed harvest, a war in a distant region or a sudden jump in the price of fuel. Moreover, where most money takes the form of bank deposits that pay interest, and where that interest rises when inflation rises, the revenue a state gains from mild inflation is modest. To describe every increase in prices as a tax is to attribute intention and gain in cases where there may be neither.

What the old idea gets right is the question it trains us to ask: who gains? When inflation is high and persistent and the state is a heavy debtor, the answer frequently points to the treasury, and the language of taxation is then not rhetoric but accurate description. When inflation is mild, or arrives from abroad through the price of imports, the same language obscures more than it reveals. The concept of an inflation tax is best treated as a tool of diagnosis rather than as a verdict reached in advance.

passage: Indirect rule was presented by its architects as an act of restraint. Rather than replace the institutions of the peoples it governed, the colonial state would work through them: chiefs would keep their offices, customary courts would apply customary law, and the colonial officer would advise rather than command. The policy, most closely associated with British administration in Nigeria and later extended across much of British Africa, was cheaper than direct administration, and its defenders also claimed for it a moral advantage. It would let colonised peoples develop along their own lines instead of being turned into imitation Europeans.

The difficulty was that the institutions indirect rule claimed to preserve rarely existed in the form it required. The policy needed a chief: one identifiable person in each locality who could collect tax, supply labour and answer for order. Where centralised kingdoms existed, such a figure could be found. Where authority had been spread among councils of elders, age-grades and religious associations, as in parts of south-eastern Nigeria, officials appointed men to the role, and the so-called warrant chiefs they created had little standing in local tradition. Even where genuine rulers existed, their position changed. A king who had once had to keep the support of title-holders and rivals, and who faced the threat that subjects might desert him, now had the backing of a colonial army, and the checks that had limited him lost much of their force.

Customary law underwent a similar transformation. To be applied in courts, custom had to be written down, and the people asked to state it were usually senior men with an interest in the answer. Rules about land, marriage and inheritance that had been flexible and contested were recorded as fixed, and frequently in the form most favourable to elders against juniors and men against women. Custom that had changed with circumstances became a code that could be changed only by the administration.

It would be wrong, however, to conclude that tradition was simply invented by colonial officials and imposed on passive subjects. The elders who told officers what the custom was were pursuing their own ends, and they often succeeded; the codes bear their fingerprints as much as the administrators'. That is precisely what makes indirect rule instructive. Its most lasting effect was not the preservation of old authority, nor its outright replacement, but the creation of a new kind of authority that spoke the language of tradition while answering upward to the state rather than downward to the governed. Many post-colonial governments, finding such authority convenient, kept it.

passage: That most citizens know little about the policies they vote on is one of the most frequently confirmed observations about modern democracies, and one of the least surprising. A single vote almost never decides an election, and the hours needed to master the details of tax law or trade policy are hours taken from work, family and sleep. Ignorance, in these circumstances, is not a failure of character. It is what a sensible person would choose if he or she treated the vote as a decision with private costs and a vanishingly small chance of making a difference. Economists call this rational ignorance, and the label is apt: the problem is not that voters reason badly but that they have little reason to acquire what good reasoning would need.

Two very different conclusions are drawn from this. The first, which has gained a certain academic following, is that the franchise should be weighted towards those who know more, since a decision made by the informed is likely to be better than one made by everyone. The second, more common among defenders of democracy, is that ignorance matters less than it seems, because voters rely on shortcuts. They need not study a programme if they know which party proposed it; they need not understand monetary policy to notice whether prices are rising; they can follow the advice of an organisation they trust. A voter equipped with such cues, the argument goes, can vote much as she would if she were fully informed.

The second conclusion is more attractive than the first, but it claims too much. A shortcut is only as good as the connection between the cue and the thing the voter actually cares about, and that connection is not guaranteed. Party labels are informative when parties are stable and their programmes distinct; when parties fragment or converge, the label says little. Judging a government by how things are going is reasonable if the government controls how things are going, but voters who punish an incumbent for a drought, or for a downturn that began abroad, are using a cue that measures luck as much as competence. And an endorsement is valuable only if the endorser shares the voter's interests, which is precisely what a well-funded campaign may try to disguise. Shortcuts, in short, do not make ignorance harmless; they make its effects depend on the environment in which voters find themselves.

That dependence, however, is also the strongest reply to those who would ration the vote. If the quality of popular judgement varies with the reliability of the cues available, then the natural remedy is to improve the cues rather than to disqualify the people who use them. Parties with clear and lasting identities, intermediaries whose interests are visible, a press that reports what governments actually control: each of these makes ordinary shortcuts more trustworthy. Weighting votes by knowledge, by contrast, would leave the environment of cues untouched while inviting a quarrel, unlikely ever to be settled impartially, about who should set the test and what it should contain.

Neither side, then, has quite grasped the problem. The critics are right that an uninformed electorate can be misled, and the defenders are right that citizens need not be experts to judge well. What both overlook is that the competence of voters is not a fixed property of individuals but partly a product of institutions, and that a democracy can therefore make its citizens wiser as voters without making any of them more learned.

passage: Among professional historians it has become something of a reflex to sneer at heritage. The restored cottage with its costumed guide, the festival that re-enacts a battle every summer, the gift shop selling replica coins and the television drama in which everyone has perfect teeth are all, on this view, so many falsifications: a past made comfortable, sold by the ticket and stripped of everything that might disturb a family on a day out. The critics are not wrong about the facts. Heritage does select, simplify and flatter, and it usually offers the past with the smell taken out.

What the critique misses is that heritage is not attempting to be history and failing at it. The two draw on the same materials, the same buildings, objects and stories, but they put them to different uses. History asks questions of the past and follows the evidence wherever it leads, including towards conclusions that unsettle the people who hear them. Heritage asks the past to confirm something about the present: that this town has deep roots, that this people has endured, that the place where one lives is worth caring about. Its characteristic question is not 'what happened here, and why?' but 'why should this place and its people matter to us?', and its characteristic answer is an experience rather than an argument. It is closer to commemoration than to inquiry, and it should be judged as commemoration is judged.

Consider a family that marks a grandparent's long marriage with a party, old photographs on the walls and affectionate speeches. Nobody expects the speeches to include an account of the couple's worst quarrels, and nobody thinks the omission a lie; the occasion exists to celebrate, and everyone present understands this. The tidying that heritage performs is, in the same way, not itself the offence. A restored village that shows thatched roofs and spinning wheels but not the open drains or the cramped rooms where servants slept is doing what celebrations do. There is even a case that it does history a service, for many people first sense that the past was inhabited by real people when they stand in such a room, and the curiosity awakened there leads some of them on to the harder questions that history asks.

The trouble begins at a specific point, and it is worth locating precisely. It comes when heritage claims the authority of history: when a site presents its selective story not as a celebration but as an account of how things really were, when a guidebook dismisses awkward evidence as the invention of cynics, or when public money that once sustained archives and libraries is redirected to attractions that will draw larger crowds. A museum label that calls a disputed episode 'settled', or a re-enactment whose script quietly drops the side that lost, does more than simplify; it borrows the standing of scholarship in order to close a question that scholarship has left open. At that point celebration has stopped being one use of the past among others and has begun to crowd out the use that tests it.

The sensible relation between the two is neither contempt nor merger. History should remain the critic of heritage, ready to point out what a display leaves out and to say so in public; heritage can remain what it is, a doorway through which many people first enter the past. The line that needs defending is not the one between the professional and the popular, but the one between celebration that knows itself to be celebration and celebration that presents itself as knowledge.

passage: For much of the last century it was an article of faith among progressive architects that ornament was a kind of lie. A building, they argued, should declare its structure and its purpose plainly; carving and moulding added cost without adding use, and they disguised what a building really was beneath a costume borrowed from some other age. The argument had moral force, and it produced buildings of great clarity. It also rested on a narrow idea of what counts as use.

Consider what ornament has traditionally done: a carved surround tells a stranger which of many openings is the entrance, so that nobody needs to read a sign to find the way in. A band of moulding at the level of the first floor breaks a tall wall into parts that a human eye can measure, so that a passer-by senses the height of the building in storeys rather than as an undifferentiated cliff. Projecting mouldings over windows throw rain clear of the glass and, as they weather, gather their stains in a pattern that reads as intended rather than as decay. Even purely figurative ornament, a row of leaves or a face above a door, offers the eye something to rest on at walking pace, which is the pace at which most people meet most buildings. These are uses, though not of the kind that appear in a structural calculation.

The critics were right about one thing: ornament applied without regard to any of these purposes, stuck on to a facade like a label on a jar, is as dishonest as they said, and much commercial building of their day was exactly that. But the remedy they chose, to strip surfaces bare, threw away the work along with the pretence. A blank wall is not neutral, for it tells the stranger nothing about where to go in, it offers no measure of scale, and it weathers into streaks that look like neglect because nothing in its design anticipated them. The plain building is honest about its structure and silent about almost everything else that a person on the street needs to know.

The more useful question, then, is not whether a building should be ornamented but what its ornament is for. Asked in that way, the question rules out a good deal of pastiche, the reproduction of historical detail for its associations alone. It also rules out a good deal of austerity that passes itself off as rigour, and it returns the judgement of a facade to the people who have to find their way past it.

passage: For a generation, the managers of manufacturing firms were taught to regard inventory as waste. Parts sitting in a warehouse tie up money, take up space and conceal problems that a tighter system would expose, so the ideal was to have each component arrive just as it was needed, often from a single supplier chosen because it was the cheapest or the best. Applied across borders, this logic produced supply chains of remarkable length and precision, in which a product might cross several frontiers as it was assembled, with little stock held at any stage.

The gains were real, and it would be a mistake to dismiss them in hindsight. Lower costs reached consumers as lower prices, and firms in poorer countries gained access to markets they could not otherwise have entered. But a system tuned to perform well under normal conditions can perform very badly under abnormal ones. When a single factory, port or region on which many chains depend is shut by a fire, a flood or a closed border, there is no slack anywhere to absorb the shock, and the shortage of one cheap part can halt the assembly of goods worth thousands of times as much.

A popular response is to call for production to be brought home. The instinct is understandable, but as a remedy for fragility it is oddly chosen. A chain that depends on one domestic plant is no less exposed to a single fire or flood than one that depends on a single foreign plant; it has merely moved its point of failure to a place that feels more familiar. What protects against disruption is not proximity but redundancy: more than one supplier for critical parts, suppliers in places unlikely to suffer the same shock at the same time, and stocks large enough to bridge an interruption.

Redundancy, however, costs money, which is precisely why lean systems eliminated it. A firm deciding how much spare capacity to keep weighs the expense against its own expected losses from a disruption, but some of the losses fall on others: on patients who cannot obtain a medicine, on other firms whose lines stop, on workers sent home without pay. Because these costs do not appear in the firm's accounts, it will tend to hold less insurance than would be sensible for the economy as a whole. The real question, then, is not where things are made but who pays for the resilience that markets left to themselves will tend to supply too sparingly.

passage: We tend to speak of forgetting as a failure, the mind's equivalent of a leaking roof: students blame it for poor marks, older people fear it as a sign of decline, and whole industries promise to reduce it. Behind these attitudes lies an assumption that an ideal memory would keep everything. Even our vocabulary betrays the attitude, since we speak of 'losing' a memory as though it were a possession that had slipped out of a pocket. It is worth asking whether the assumption behind such talk is true.

Consider what such a memory would be like to live with. Every time you parked your car, you would recall not only today's space but every space you had ever used, each with equal force. Every time you met a friend, you would be confronted with each version of her face across the years. The problem would not be a shortage of information but a surplus of it, because the memory you needed would be buried among the memories you did not. Some people who report unusually complete recall of their own lives describe the gift less as a pleasure than as a burden, a past that will not stay in the past.

Seen in this light, much forgetting looks less like decay than like editing. Memories that are rarely used become harder to reach, while those that are used often stay accessible, and the effect is less a loss than a reordering of priorities. This is roughly what a sensible filing system would do: it would keep the files you consult near at hand and move the rest to the back, on the reasonable bet that the past use of a memory predicts its future use. Some evidence even suggests that recalling one memory actively suppresses its competitors, so that using your new phone number makes the old one fade faster.

This argument has limits, and it is easy to push it too far, for not all forgetting is useful: the losses caused by brain injury or dementia are not editing but damage, and nothing said here makes them less painful. Nor does a system that is well designed on average serve every individual case: the name you cannot recall at an important meeting is a real cost, even if it is the price of a sensible policy. The point is only that the capacity to forget is part of what makes memory useful, not simply a flaw in it. A memory that never let go would be a worse memory, not a better one.

passage: Inquiries into industrial disasters have a way of finding a culprit. An operator ignored a warning, an inspector signed a form he had not read, a manager overruled an engineer whose objections were inconvenient. Such findings are rarely false, but they are often beside the point, because they treat as a single failure of judgement what was in fact the end of a long and orderly process. Many organisations do not stumble into catastrophe; they walk towards it by steps that each seemed reasonable at the time.

Consider a hypothetical chemical plant whose procedures say that a certain vessel must be shut down if its pressure exceeds a stated limit. One night the gauge registers a reading marginally above the permitted limit. Shutting down would be expensive, the excess is small, and the engineers on duty judge, correctly as it turns out, that the vessel is in no danger. Nothing untoward happens, and the next time the reading creeps over the limit there is a precedent, which makes the decision considerably easier. After a dozen such nights the limit has quietly moved: the written figure still stands in the manual, but the working figure, the one people actually act on, is higher. No one decided to change it. The change was made by the accumulated absence of harm.

This is what makes the process so difficult to detect from within the organisation itself. Each step is defended by evidence, and the evidence is genuine, for the vessel really did not fail. What is mistaken is the inference drawn from it, that a risk which has not yet produced harm has thereby been shown to be small. Success becomes a reason for confidence, and confidence a reason to look less closely, so that the organisation's sense of its own safety grows at the same rate as its actual exposure to danger. By the time an outsider asks why the plant routinely runs above its limit, the question sounds naive, because everyone inside knows that it always has.

It does not follow that every departure from the rules is a step towards disaster. Written procedures are drafted in advance by people who cannot foresee every situation, and an organisation whose staff never deviated from them would be unable to adapt; much good practice begins as a sensible exception. The danger lies not in deviation itself but in deviation that is never recognised as such. A departure that is noticed, argued over and formally adopted is a decision; one that simply accumulates is drift, and drift answers to no one.

passage: A long tradition explains exceptional performance by talent: the chess master and the concert violinist are thought to have been born with something the rest of us lack. A body of research on practice has done much to unsettle this view. Those who reach the top of skilled fields, it turns out, have typically spent very large amounts of time not merely doing the activity but practising it in a particular way: working on specific weaknesses, at the edge of their current ability, with prompt feedback, usually under the eye of a teacher. Experience alone, on this account, is not enough. A person who has driven a car for twenty years has had a great deal of experience but has probably not improved since the first few, because ordinary driving involves no deliberate effort to get better.

The strongest version of this view holds that practice of the right kind is not just necessary for expertise but very nearly sufficient, so that differences in accumulated practice explain most of the differences between the great and the merely good. Popularised as a rule that a fixed number of hours will make anyone an expert, it has an obvious democratic appeal. It is also, in that form, hard to sustain. Among people who practise a great deal, the amount of practice leaves much of the variation in performance unexplained, and the size of that unexplained remainder seems to differ across domains. Where the rules are stable and feedback is immediate, as in many games and sports, practice accounts for more; where outcomes are delayed and noisy, as in forecasting markets or judging which patient will recover, it accounts for less.

This last pattern is revealing, because it suggests that what practice builds depends on what the environment can teach. Deliberate practice requires knowing, quickly and reliably, whether an attempt succeeded. A violinist hears a wrong note at once; a chess player can check a line against a stronger opponent. A financial analyst may wait years to learn whether a judgement was sound, and even then the outcome will reflect luck as much as skill. In such fields long careers can produce confidence without accuracy, and the hours a person has logged may say more about seniority than about expertise.

None of this restores the old picture of talent as a fixed endowment that settles everything. The research on practice was right that expertise is built rather than found, and right that the manner of practice matters more than its sheer quantity. What it cannot do is deliver the promise sometimes made in its name, that anyone who puts in the hours will arrive at the same place. Starting points differ, the rate at which practice pays off differs, and some fields offer so little reliable feedback that practice in the demanding sense is barely possible within them.

passage: Two drivers leave the same party, each having had one drink too many, and each drives home along the same dark road with the same degree of carelessness. The first arrives home without incident; the second, rounding a bend, strikes a child who has run into the road. Most people judge the second driver far more harshly than the first: he may face prison, while the first, if caught at all, will pay a fine, and the second driver himself will probably carry a burden of guilt that the first never feels. Yet the only difference between them is something neither of them controlled, namely whether a child happened to be on the road at that moment.

Philosophers call this resultant moral luck, and it presents a genuine puzzle. A widely held principle says that we should be blamed only for what lies within our control. If that principle is right, the two drivers deserve exactly the same blame, since their choices, their states of mind and their recklessness were identical. Our differing reactions must then be a mistake, an emotional response to a dreadful outcome that we wrongly dress up as a moral judgement. On this view, the honest course is to blame both drivers equally, and severely, for the risk each of them imposed on others.

This conclusion is tidy, but I think it is too quick, because it treats our responses to outcomes as noise to be filtered out when they may be tracking something real. The second driver has done something the first has not: he has killed a child. His relationship to the child's family, to the world and to his own past is altered in a way that the first driver's is not. To feel and to judge that he must answer for this is not simply to confuse bad luck with bad character. It reflects the fact that agency extends into the world, and that what we are responsible for includes, in part, what our actions actually bring about.

None of this licenses the opposite error of treating the lucky driver as blameless. He did something seriously wrong, and the fact that his drive ended well is no credit to him. The point is narrower: the control principle captures one important strand of our thinking about blame, the strand concerned with assessing character and choice, but it is not the whole of moral life. A theory that cannot make sense of why the second driver should apologise to the family, and why the first has no one to apologise to, has not purified our moral concepts; it has impoverished them.

passage: The laws of war rest on a premise that, stated baldly, can seem scandalous. A soldier who fights for an aggressor and a soldier who fights to repel him are held to have exactly the same rights on the battlefield: each may lawfully kill enemy combatants, each must spare civilians and prisoners, and neither commits a crime merely by taking part. Whether the war itself was just, a question settled, if at all, by the cause for which it was begun, is treated as irrelevant to how it may be fought. The justice of going to war and justice in the conduct of war are kept in separate compartments, and the ordinary soldier is answerable only for the second.

Philosophical critics have pressed hard on this separation, and their central argument is difficult to resist. Outside war, we do not think that someone who attacks without justification acquires a right to kill those who resist him; a robber who is fired on by the guard he is trying to overpower may not shoot back and call it self-defence. Why should the matter change when the attacker wears a uniform and acts on orders? If the right to kill in war derives, as it must, from the right to defend against an unjust threat, then those who pose the unjust threat seem to have no such right at all. On this view, the soldier of an aggressor state who kills a defending soldier does wrong, however scrupulously he observes the rules of conduct.

I think the critics are right about the underlying morality and wrong about what follows for the laws of war. Rules for the conduct of hostilities must be followed by people who are frightened, poorly informed and dependent on their own government's account of why they are fighting. Nearly every belligerent believes, or is told, that its cause is just. A rule that granted the right to kill only to soldiers on the just side would therefore be claimed by both sides, and would offer no restraint precisely where restraint is most needed; worse, it would invite each side to treat captured enemies as criminals rather than as prisoners. The symmetry of the laws of war is not a judgement that both sides are equally innocent. It is a convention adopted because the alternative would make war more savage without making it more just.

Conceding this does not license the conclusion that soldiers bear no responsibility for the wars they fight. A convention that withholds legal blame is not a certificate of moral innocence, and there will be wars whose injustice is so plain that an ordinary soldier could see it and ought to refuse. The doctrine of equality is best understood not as a truth about the morality of killing but as a practical arrangement that we maintain, knowingly, because it does more to limit the horror of war than any rule that tracked the moral truth more closely could do.

passage: For most of its history the word 'computer' named an occupation rather than a machine. Observatories, survey offices and, later, engineering firms employed rooms of people whose work consisted of carrying out long calculations, often for tables of positions, tides or trajectories that others would use. It is tempting to treat these workers as a quaint prelude to the real story, a stopgap that lasted only until electronics arrived. That reading gets the relation backwards. The electronic computer did not introduce the idea of mechanical calculation into a world that lacked it; it inherited an idea that human computing offices had already worked out in detail.

The key feature of such offices was not the arithmetic skill of any individual but the way the work was organised. A planner with mathematical training would break a difficult problem into a sequence of simple steps, write those steps on printed sheets, and hand the sheets to workers who needed to know only how to add, subtract and look up values in a table. The workers did not have to understand why a step was there, and the scheme was in fact designed so that they would not need to. Errors were caught not by insight but by procedure: two people would compute the same column independently, and any disagreement sent the column back. What was being built, in effect, was a method in which correctness no longer depended on anyone grasping the whole.

Seen this way, much of what we think of as distinctive about programming was already present. The separation between the person who designs a procedure and the agent who executes it, the reduction of judgement to rules, the checking of results by redundancy rather than by understanding: all of these were practices before they were properties of machines. When the first electronic machines were built, their designers could borrow not only mathematical techniques from the computing offices but also a whole conception of what it meant to make a calculation reliable.

None of this is to say that the machines merely did faster what people had done slowly. Speed of the magnitude electronics provided changed which problems were worth posing at all; calculations that would have occupied a room of workers for years became routine, and whole fields grew up around them. But the continuity matters, because it reminds us that the habit of treating thought as something that can be divided, written down and handed to an executor who need not understand it is a social invention before it is a technical one. Its consequences, good and bad, were visible in offices long before they were visible on screens.

passage: Among the people who first tried to build thinking machines, a surprise emerged that has never quite been absorbed. The tasks that seemed to demand the most intelligence, such as proving theorems, playing chess or solving problems in algebra, turned out to be comparatively tractable for computers, while tasks that any small child performs without effort, such as recognising a face across a room, picking up an unfamiliar object or walking over uneven ground, proved stubbornly hard. The observation is often associated with the roboticist Hans Moravec, and it is usually called a paradox. Whether it deserves the name depends on what we took difficulty to be in the first place.

The most common explanation is evolutionary. Seeing, grasping and moving have been refined over hundreds of millions of years of animal life, and the machinery that performs them is vast, ancient and almost entirely hidden from awareness. Abstract reasoning, by contrast, is a recent arrival, practised deliberately and with effort. We notice the effort and conclude that reasoning is hard; we notice nothing when we recognise a friend's face, and conclude that perception is easy. On this account the paradox is an artefact of introspection: our sense of difficulty tracks how much of a skill reaches consciousness, not how much computation it requires.

This explanation is persuasive, but it should not be stretched into the claim that every skill we find effortless is computationally deep, or that every skill we find laborious is shallow. Some effortless skills may be easy for machines too, and some laborious ones, like long division, are trivial for any pocket calculator while others remain hard. The evolutionary story explains a general tendency; it does not supply a rule. Nor has the gap stood still. Machines have become far better at recognising images and speech than early researchers expected, though a robot that can fold an unfamiliar garment or clear an untidy table remains much harder to build than a program that plays chess at a master's level.

The deeper lesson concerns our idea of intelligence itself. For a long time intelligence was identified with the activities that educated adults found hardest and prized most: calculation, logic, formal games. The paradox suggests that this identification was parochial. What humans find hard is a measure of human limitations, not a measure of how much intelligence a task needs, and the competences we share with other animals may contain more of what is difficult about minds than the competences that distinguish us. A cat crossing a cluttered shelf without disturbing anything is solving problems that our best machines still find formidable, and it would be odd to call that achievement unintelligent merely because no cat could sit an examination.

passage: Imagine a photograph of a cat staring with great solemnity at an empty food bowl. In its first appearance the caption beneath it complains, in the cat's voice, about a late breakfast. Within days the same photograph carries hundreds of other captions: a student staring at an exam paper, an investor staring at a falling share price, a voter staring at a ballot. The cat, and the bowl, have stopped meaning anything about cats. They have become a frame into which almost any experience of disappointed expectation can be placed.

This is the ordinary life of an internet meme, and it is worth noticing what has actually spread. It is not a message, since the messages are all different and many contradict one another. What has spread is a template: a recognisable structure with a slot in it, together with a tacit rule about what kind of thing goes in the slot. Those who share the meme are not endorsing a claim; they are demonstrating that they know the form and can fill it aptly. The pleasure is the pleasure of a good fit, much like the pleasure an audience once took in a skilled performer's handling of a familiar tale, where the interest lay less in what happened than in how well the expected moves were made.

This has consequences for how memes are read by those who study public opinion. It is tempting to treat the reach of a political meme as a measure of agreement with it, as if each share were a small vote. But a template can carry a sentiment its sharers do not hold, simply because the sentiment fits the slot neatly, and a meme that mocks one side may be passed along by the other side in an inverted version that keeps the frame and reverses the point. Counting shares, in such cases, measures the vitality of the form far more reliably than the distribution of belief.

It would be too quick to conclude that memes persuade nobody. Repetition has effects, and a frame that is used often enough can make one way of seeing a situation feel natural before anyone has argued for it. If the cat's bowl is used a thousand times to describe a particular government's policies, the idea that those policies are a disappointment may come to seem like common knowledge. But the persuasive power, where it exists, lies in the frame's quiet familiarity rather than in any argument, and it is precisely because memes do not look like arguments that their influence is so hard to measure and so easy to misread.

passage: The founders of modern geology won their central argument so completely that its terms are now remembered mainly as a caricature. Against older accounts that explained mountains, valleys and buried shells by a few vast upheavals, they proposed that the Earth's features had been shaped by the same slow processes that can be watched today: rivers cutting their beds, waves wearing down cliffs, sediment settling grain by grain on the floors of lakes and seas. Given enough time, such ordinary causes could account for extraordinary results, and the immense age of the Earth that this view required became one of its most consequential implications. The doctrine came to be called uniformitarianism, and its rival, the appeal to sudden and violent change, catastrophism. In the familiar telling, patient observation defeated speculation.

The telling is unfair to both sides. Uniformitarianism bundled together several claims of very different standing. One was that the laws of nature have not changed, so that water flowed and rock fractured in the past as it does now. Another was methodological: that a geologist should first try to explain the record by causes known to operate, and invoke unobserved ones only when those fail. A third was a claim about the Earth itself, that change had generally proceeded at gentle and roughly steady rates. The first two are close to the preconditions of any historical science. The third is an empirical hypothesis, and it could have turned out false.

In part, it did. Through much of the twentieth century, geologists who proposed sudden events of enormous scale met resistance out of proportion to their evidence. A landscape of deep channels and giant ripples in the north-western United States was long attributed to ordinary erosion before it was accepted as the work of floods released when ice dams failed; the suggestion that the mass extinction at the end of the age of dinosaurs followed the impact of a large asteroid met at first with widespread doubt, some of it dismissive. In both cases the objection was less that the evidence was weak than that the explanation sounded like the discredited catastrophism of the past. A rule of method, prefer known causes, had hardened into a belief about what the Earth was permitted to have done.

It would be wrong, however, to conclude that the old suspicion of catastrophes was mere prejudice. Many early catastrophist explanations could not be tested: they posited events of unspecified cause that left no trace except the very features they were invoked to explain. Against such accounts, a demand for known causes was a reasonable discipline, and it is part of why the later catastrophes were eventually accepted. The flood hypothesis prevailed when the lake held back by the ice and the shorelines it left were identified; the impact hypothesis prevailed when a thin layer rich in a rare metal was traced around the world and a buried crater of the right age was found. What persuaded geologists was not a relaxation of the old standard but evidence that met it.

The view that now prevails keeps the uniformity of laws and the preference for testable causes while abandoning the assumption of uniform rates. The Earth's history includes long stretches of slow change punctuated by rare events of great violence, and both are explained by the same physics; neither the slow nor the violent is an exception that must apologise for itself. The lesson reaches beyond geology. A principle adopted to keep inquiry honest can, if it is mistaken for a description of the world, end by closing questions it was meant to keep open.

passage: Historians trained on written records have long treated oral testimony with suspicion, and their reasons are not foolish. Memories fade and are reshaped by everything that happened afterwards; a speaker recalling events of fifty years ago has also absorbed fifty years of conversation, newspapers and family retelling, and cannot always tell what she saw from what she later heard. Anyone who has compared an elderly person's account of a local event with the surviving paperwork knows how often the dates, the sequence and even the participants differ. As a chronicle of what happened and when, the spoken memory of a single witness is frequently unreliable.

The objection assumes, however, that the only purpose of testimony is to establish what happened. Consider a hypothetical mining town in which many older residents, interviewed separately, place a bitter strike in the same year as a disastrous flood, although the records show that the two events were several years apart. As evidence about dates, these accounts are simply wrong. As evidence about how the town came to understand its own past, they are remarkably revealing, for the merging of the two events suggests that residents experienced them as a single catastrophe, perhaps because in both the company that owned the mine was felt to have abandoned them.

The crucial point is that shared and patterned errors are not the same as noise. Individual slips of memory are scattered more or less at random; one witness misplaces a year, another confuses two neighbours. When many people independently make the same mistake, however, the mistake becomes a social fact, something that calls for explanation rather than mere correction. And patterned error of this kind is precisely what written records cannot supply, because documents tend to record events, while the meanings that people attached to those events, and the way those meanings settled over decades, rarely find their way into an official file.

None of this licenses the historian to treat every inaccuracy as meaningful or to abandon the ordinary work of checking. An error can be interpreted only once it has been established that it is an error, and that usually requires the very documents that oral historians are sometimes too quick to dismiss. The strongest work therefore uses the two kinds of source together, letting each expose what the other cannot see: the record correcting the memory, and the memory revealing what the record left out.

passage: Introducing video review into professional sport seemed to settle an old grievance. For as long as games have had officials, players and spectators have complained that decisions were wrong, and now there was a technology that could show, from several angles and at any speed, what had really happened. Few people expected that the result would be a new and more corrosive kind of dispute. Yet that is what many supporters now describe: arguments that once ended with the whistle continue through slow-motion replays, frozen frames and lines drawn on screens, and they seem less settled than before.

The puzzle dissolves once we ask what the referee's authority was for. It was never simply a matter of being right. A match needs some means of converting a contested event into a settled fact quickly enough for play to continue, and the referee supplied it by being final. Players accepted decisions they believed mistaken not because they trusted the official's eyesight but because they had accepted, in joining the game, that someone must decide and that the decision would stand. Error was tolerated as the price of finality, and since the errors fell, over a season, on all sides alike, the price seemed bearable.

Review alters this bargain in two ways. First, it relocates authority. The decision now seems to belong to the replay, and the referee on the field becomes a provisional judge whose rulings await confirmation from elsewhere. Second, and less obviously, it changes the kind of question being asked. Whether a challenge was reckless, or whether an attacker gained an advantage, is a matter of judgement that a trained official can make in a moment. Whether a toe was ahead of a defender's shoulder at the instant the ball was struck is presented as a matter of fact, yet the answer depends on which frame is chosen and where the line is drawn, choices that the apparent precision of the image conceals. A decision dressed as measurement invites challenge in a way that an acknowledged judgement does not, because every measurement can be disputed by another.

None of this is a case for abandoning the cameras. A goal awarded for a shot that plainly missed, or a player sent off for a foul committed by someone else, is an injustice that no appeal to finality can make acceptable, and replays remove such errors cheaply. The mistake lies in treating review as a means of perfecting every marginal call. Confined to clear and obvious errors, it supports the referee's authority; extended to the margins, it dissolves the very finality that made officiating possible.

passage: It is natural to think of seeing as a kind of recording. Light enters the eye, an image forms on the retina, and the brain, like a careful clerk, reads off what is there. The picture is attractive because it matches how perception feels: effortless, immediate, and apparently free of any contribution from the perceiver. Yet the retinal image is a poor document: it is upside down, flat, constantly jittering with the movements of the eye, and interrupted by a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina. Above all, it is ambiguous, in the sense that a small image on the retina could be a small object nearby or a large one far away; a patch of dim grey could be a dark surface in bright light or a pale surface in shadow. The eye, in short, delivers considerably less information than we ordinarily experience ourselves as seeing.

For this reason many students of vision have preferred to describe perception as a form of inference. The brain, on this account, treats the incoming signal as evidence and settles on the interpretation that best explains it, given what it has learned about how the world usually is. Light tends to come from above, so a disc shaded darker at the bottom is seen as a bump and the same disc turned over as a dent. Objects tend to keep their size, so a person walking away is seen as receding rather than shrinking. These are not conclusions we reach; they are conclusions reached on our behalf, before anything is presented to awareness.

The word 'inference' invites an obvious objection: if perception is a guess shaped by expectation, why do we not simply see whatever we expect? The answer is that the guess is tightly disciplined by the evidence, and that the expectations doing the work are of a peculiar kind. They are not the beliefs we hold and can revise in conversation, but assumptions built up over a lifetime of looking, and perhaps over the history of the species. This is why many visual illusions survive full knowledge of the trick. A viewer who has measured two lines and found them equal will still see one as longer; what she knows and what she sees have been settled by different processes.

It would be a mistake, then, to conclude that perception is unreliable because it is inferential. The assumptions it relies on are mostly true of the environments in which they were formed, which is why they so rarely mislead us outside the laboratory, where illusions are carefully built to exploit them. What the inferential view really overturns is not our trust in the senses but the idea that seeing is passive. Every glance is a small act of interpretation, and its seeming effortlessness is the mark of how well the work is done, not evidence that no work is being done.
